s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: A European word meaning "eastern," revived in the 19th century, is used broadly for which architectural tradition?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 6–7: Definition of Terms — Saracenic Architecture
n: Saracenic is a European term meaning eastern and denotes Muslim architecture in general — more especially the Arab style of Muslim architecture. It was revived in the 19th century.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Rooted in the idea that people are innately drawn to connect with nature — but without making a building visually resemble nature itself — which design approach is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Biophilic; Biomorphic Design
n: Biophilic design comes from the "biophilia hypothesis" and targets human experience and physiological well-being inside the space. Biomorphic design is the contrast the reviewer draws: it is primarily formal and aesthetic, borrowing the shapes of living organisms.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: What term names the idea that architecture ought to reflect the cultural and technological spirit of the era in which it is produced?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Zeitgeist (Hegel & Giedion, Space, Time and Architecture)
n: Zeitgeist is the "spirit of the times," credited here to Hegel and to Giedion's Space, Time and Architecture. Genius loci is the near miss — it concerns the spirit of a place, not of an era.

s: Historical Development — Contemporary Theory (21st Century)
q: In which decade did the arrival of CAD and, later, more advanced computational tools transform architectural theory and practice?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 11–12: Contemporary Theory: Digital Architecture and Parametricism
n: The reviewer places the revolution in the 1990s. Architects began exploring forms previously unbuildable, and theory developed around genetic algorithms, emergence, and parametric variation.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: A flat-roofed white residence near Paris, raised on slender pilotis with horizontal ribbon windows and an open plan, stands as the model International Style house — which building is it?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Villa Savoye (1929–31) near Paris is the exemplary International Style residence. The Tugendhat and Farnsworth houses are Mies's, and the Vanna Venturi House is a postmodern rebuttal to precisely this kind of building.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: Charles-Edouard Jeanneret was the birth name of which prominent early figure of the International Style?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 12–13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Charles-Edouard Jeanneret is Le Corbusier. In the 1920s he formulated his Five Points of Architecture and proclaimed "a house is a machine for living in."

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: In postmodern practice, reinterpreting classical elements with "playful historicism" means treating them in what manner?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: Playful historicism reinterprets classical elements with wit and irony. Archaeological accuracy is exactly what 19th-century revivalism aimed at and what postmodernism deliberately declined.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: During the 1910s and 1920s, Spanish Colonial Revival was practiced especially in which U.S. state?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Spanish Colonial Revival
n: The reviewer places Spanish Colonial Revival particularly in California during the 1910s and 1920s. It reuses colonial styles brought by Spanish settlers to Latin America and the southwestern United States in the 17th and 18th centuries, and is sometimes called the Spanish Revival or Spanish style.

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: The theoretical evolution of medieval architecture is tied to the development of which three structural elements?
o: The pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and the flying buttress
The round arch, the groin vault, and the buttress pier
The ogee curve, the ribbed vault, and the pinnacle
The pointed arch, the barrel vault, and the pilaster
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period
n: The pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and the flying buttress. The reviewer's point is that the "theory" was the engineering itself — achieving height and light to represent the Heavenly Jerusalem.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: Which pair of works exemplifies Mies van der Rohe's extreme clarity and "less is more" minimalism, with one described as epitomizing the modernist domestic ideal?
o: The Fagus Factory (1911) and the Bauhaus building
The Seagram Building (1958) and the Farnsworth House
The Barcelona Pavilion (1929) and the Tugendhat House (1930)
The Lever House (1952) and the IIT campus
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: The Barcelona Pavilion (1929) and the Tugendhat House (1930); the reviewer quotes the latter as having "epitomized the modernist domestic setting at its best."

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Marked by a taste for the informal and vernacular, which early 20th-century Scandinavian movement, especially strong in Sweden, is being described?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — National Romanticism
n: National Romanticism was the Scandinavian movement, particularly strong in Sweden, with a taste for the informal and the vernacular.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Buildings intentionally designed to resemble inanimate man-made objects, typically for advertising purposes, fall under which category — sometimes also termed Mimetic architecture?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Novelty Architecture
n: Novelty architecture, often called Mimetic architecture, features buildings designed to look like inanimate, man-made objects, usually for advertising or commercial purposes.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: With the 1972 demolition of which project did Jencks proclaim the "death of modernism"?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Charles Jencks
n: The demolition of the Pruitt-Igoe housing project in 1972 is the event Jencks used to declare modernism dead. He promoted instead an architecture communicating meaning through symbols and context.

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: Abbot Suger's renovation of which building is credited with introducing Gothic architecture?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period: Abbot Suger
n: Abbot Suger (c. 1081–1151) introduced Gothic architecture through the renovation of the Basilica of Saint-Denis, focusing on light and height as metaphysical elements connecting man with God.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: For a 1932 MoMA exhibition, which pair coined the term "International Style"?
o: Walter Gropius and Mies van der Rohe
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Henry-Russell Hitchcock and Philip Johnson coined the term for the 1932 MoMA exhibition, by which time the Modern Movement had distilled into the style.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: The severity of form in Neoclassical architecture is described as a reaction against which earlier 18th-century style?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Neoclassical Architecture
n: Neoclassical architecture shows a formal or correct use of elements and an overall severity of form, set against the more expressive rococo style of the 18th century.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: Who is credited with coining the term "Parametricism" to describe the fluid geometries seen in Zaha Hadid's later work?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends: Digital and Parametric Design
n: Architect Patrik Schumacher dubbed the style "Parametricism." The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku (2012), with its continuous swooping surfaces, is the reviewer's example.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: In postmodern practice, celebrating pluralism meant that buildings could accomplish what?
o: Be built by multiple design teams
Communicate on multiple levels and reference culture and history
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: Pluralism here means buildings communicating on multiple levels and referencing culture and history — the same instinct Jencks captured as double coding.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: By which decade had the dominance of orthodox modernism begun to show visible cracks?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: By the 1960s architects and critics grew dissatisfied with what they saw as the sterility and inhumanity of modernist environments. Postmodern architecture itself was born of that discontent in the 1970s.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Which group, organizing in the mid-1950s, brought new ideas to CIAM's 1956 meeting and contributed to the congress's eventual breakup?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Team 10
n: Team 10 was the international group of architects whose ideas at the 1956 meeting consequently influenced the breakup of CIAM.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: In place of the "purist" modern aesthetic, what did Venturi advocate for instead?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Robert Venturi
n: He favoured ambiguous and multifaceted design, arguing buildings should communicate and embrace eclecticism.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: In which century did the Sublime become a popular aesthetic concept in England and France, discussed alongside Beauty?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Sublime
n: The reviewer places the Sublime in the 18th century in England and France, where it was discussed along with Beauty and became an ideal in landscape design and the use of nature.

s: Historical Development — 19th Century: Romanticism, Historicism and the Industrial Age
q: For which two contributions is Eugene Viollet-le-Duc (1814–1879) primarily known?
o: Iron construction and the Paris arcades
Gothic restorations and rational analysis of architecture
Gothic Revival churches and moral criticism
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: 19th Century: Eugene Viollet-le-Duc
n: Viollet-le-Duc is known for Gothic restorations and the rational analysis of architecture. Ruskin is the one who supplied moral criticism, and he opposed the industrialization Viollet-le-Duc's rationalism ultimately fed.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: The Orders are described as systems of proportion governing the relationship between which two architectural elements?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period: Orders
n: The Orders — Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and others — are systems of proportion governing the relationship between columns and entablatures.

s: Historical Development — Contemporary Theory (21st Century)
q: What chiefly characterizes 21st-century architectural theory?
o: A single dominant theory of sustainability
Pluralism, with several overlapping threads and no dominant theory
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Contemporary Theory (21st Century)
n: Pluralism: no single dominant theory, but several overlapping threads reflecting rapid technological, social, and environmental changes. Architecture is no longer monolithic, and multiple discourses coexist.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: Featuring colorful surfaces and abstracted classical references such as arched windows, keystones, and pilasters, the 1982 Portland Building was designed by whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: Michael Graves designed the Portland Building (1982), applying abstracted classical references to a modern office tower.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: This reviewer notes that Baroque buildings in which two countries were more restrained than their Continental counterparts?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Baroque Architecture
n: Baroque architecture is characterised by spatial complexity, curved surfaces, and exuberance in color and sculpture — but the reviewer notes that Baroque buildings in England and France are more restrained.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Over what span of years did the Bauhaus bring together designers, craftsmen, and architects?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Bauhaus
n: The Bauhaus operated from 1919 to 1933. The 1928–1956 span belongs to CIAM, and 1917 is the founding year of De Stijl.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: Which of these is NOT listed as a hallmark of the High-Tech style?
o: Exposed services used as aesthetic features
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: Rough exposed concrete is the trademark of Brutalism, not High-Tech. The High-Tech list is visible steel frameworks, modular prefabricated elements, exposed services such as plumbing, vents, and girders, and large expanses of glass.

s: Definition of Terms — Planning and Landscape
q: Discussed in 15th- and 16th-century Italian architectural treatises, the Ideal City concept is described as having which plan type, and how often was it actually built?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Ideal City
n: Most Ideal City schemes had radial plans and few were realized. The philosophy later reemerged c. 1900 with the garden city, the City Beautiful, and the new-town movements.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: What distinction does De Re Aedificatoria (On the Art of Building) hold?
o: It is the first printed book on the orders
It is the first Renaissance architectural treatise
It is the first treatise written in the vernacular
It is the first illustrated builder's manual
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Leon Battista Alberti
n: Alberti's De Re Aedificatoria is the first Renaissance architectural treatise. Serlio's work is the one that made Vitruvian ideas accessible to craftsmen through practical illustrations.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Which two conventions do Deconstructivist forms deliberately avoid?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: Forms appear broken apart or dislocated, avoiding traditional right angles and symmetry, in a design language of fragmentation, distortion, and dynamic tension.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: From what source does the Prairie School take its name?
o: The flat landscape of the American Midwest
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Prairie School
n: The movement is named for Frank Lloyd Wright's "Prairie House" plans. It was an early-1900s American Midwest movement focused on his work.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: Writing in the 1st century BCE, who is regarded as the father of architectural theory?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period
n: Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, of the 1st century BCE, is the father of architectural theory. Alberti is the distractor to watch — he is called the "Vitruvius of the Renaissance," a different title entirely.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: Over what span of years does this reviewer date the Renaissance period?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 8–9: Renaissance Period
n: The reviewer dates the Renaissance period from the 14th to the 17th century CE.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: What name is given to Alberti's rule that nothing may be added to or removed from an appearance without destroying its harmony?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Concinnitas (Alberti, De re aedificatoria)
n: Concinnitas is Alberti's absolute and fundamental rule of appearance, stated in De re aedificatoria. Venustas is Vitruvius's term for beauty as one of three qualities, not a rule about adding or subtracting.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Put these Italian architectural periods in the order this reviewer gives: Renaissance, Mannerism, Baroque, Gothic — which sequence is correct?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms: Renaissance Architecture; Mannerism
n: Renaissance architecture followed the Gothic style, evolved into Mannerism in Italy, and eventually into the Baroque. Mannerism sits between the Renaissance and Baroque periods, never before the Renaissance.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: According to Alberti, ideal beauty was the product of what, moving beyond mere craft?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Leon Battista Alberti
n: Alberti revived classical principles and promoted ideal beauty as a product of harmony and mathematical proportion.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: The Bauhaus philosophy held that the finest design resulted from what?
o: The vision of a single master designer
Rigorous academic instruction in the orders
The combined efforts of artists, architects, and craftsmen at every stage of creation
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 10–11: Modernism: Walter Gropius
n: The Bauhaus emphasised collaboration across disciplines — the combined efforts of artists, architects, and craftsmen throughout every stage of creation — while balancing individual expression against the needs of modern society.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: What does the rise of the "starchitect" era at the turn of the century refer to?
o: Architects designing primarily for private clients
Architects becoming media personalities on television
Celebrated architects commissioned for landmark projects worldwide
Firms merging into global corporate practices
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends: Globalization and "Starchitects"
n: The starchitect era means celebrated architects being commissioned for landmark projects worldwide — a global star system rather than a media phenomenon.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which prefix is most commonly attached to Revivalism's various styles?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Revivalism
n: Revival styles are often designated with the prefix "neo" attached to a previous historical style — neo-Tudor, neo-Futurist. Its two major types are the Greek and the Gothic revivals.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Away from which two things did Postmodernism move, as this glossary frames its emergence in the late 1970s?
o: The historicism of revival styles and the rigidity of the orders
The regionalism of vernacular building and the abstraction of De Stijl
The functional aesthetic of the international style and the severity of Brutalism
The eclecticism of Beaux-Arts and the ornament of Art Deco
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms: Postmodernism
n: Postmodernism moved away from the functional aesthetic of the international style and the severity of Brutalism, favouring a return to historical references and individualised, emotionally satisfying solutions.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: In this reviewer, the noun "architectonics" frames architecture as being treated in what way?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Architectonic
n: Architectonic relates to the architecture or design of a structure, and the noun form architectonics specifically frames architecture as a science.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: By blending motifs from the Arts and Crafts movement, classicism, neoclassicism, and other styles, postmodern architecture pursued buildings that accomplished what?
o: Erased local difference in favour of a global language
Honored local history and had a unique visual appeal
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
n: The mixing of motifs was aimed at buildings that honored their local history and had a unique visual appeal. A global language of architecture is what the International Style produced — the opposite ambition.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: High-Tech design aligns with which modernist principle, albeit expressed in a more overtly technological way?
o: A house is a machine for living in
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 14–15: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: The idea was to honestly express the engineering and give architecture an industrial, "machine-age" look, aligning with the modernist dictum of truth to materials — the same principle Ruskin had argued for a century earlier on moral grounds.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which of Ching's theories places human experience and human scale at the very center of architectural design?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Anthropocentrism (Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order)
n: Anthropocentrism puts the human being at the centre as the measure of design. Phenomenology is the closest relative in this reviewer, but it concerns sensory perception of space rather than the positioning of human scale as the design centre.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Which pairing correctly matches an Art Nouveau counterpart with its country?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Art Nouveau
n: The reviewer lists Jugendstil (Germany), Secession (Austria), Stile Liberty (Italy), and Modernismo (Spain). Only the Spanish pairing is correct as written; the other three swap countries.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Across which decades was Queen Anne style domestic architecture popular in England and the United States?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Queen Anne Style
n: Queen Anne style ran from the 1870s through the 1890s in England and the United States.

s: Historical Development — Enlightenment and Neoclassicism
q: Which three elements did Laugier identify as the essentials architecture should return to?
o: The wall, the opening, and the roof
The column, the entablature, and the pediment
The arch, the vault, and the dome
The base, the shaft, and the capital
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Enlightenment & Neoclassicism: Marc-Antoine Laugier
n: The column, the entablature, and the pediment — the parts of the Primitive Hut. Laugier argued for natural simplicity, clarity of form, and logic over ornamentation.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Established in the 16th century, which Japanese residential plan incorporates a writing area within the main room?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Shoin Style
n: Shoin style incorporates a writing area into the main room of a residence, a plan established in the 16th century. Sukiya is the other Japanese term in this glossary but takes its influence from the traditional teahouse.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: What term names the notion that a building's meaning arises from its relationship to other "texts" or buildings?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Intertextuality (Jencks)
n: Intertextuality, credited to Jencks's The Language of Post-Modern Architecture, holds that a building's meaning comes from its relationship to other texts or buildings.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: Enabled by digital technology, 21st-century architecture's pluralism of styles and fusion of influences is said to be shaped by what?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
n: The reviewer names digital technology as the enabler and global challenges as the shaping force behind contemporary pluralism.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Which type of reinforced concrete did Pier Luigi Nervi invent and put to use?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Ferrocemento
n: Ferrocemento is the type of reinforced concrete invented and used by Pier Luigi Nervi.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: How did Charles Jencks characterize postmodernism?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Charles Jencks
n: In The Language of Postmodern Architecture, Jencks defines postmodernism as a "pluralistic and double-coded" approach mixing historical references with contemporary meaning. "Complex and contradictory" belongs to Venturi's title.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: Beyond the Triad, which three qualities did Vitruvius emphasize?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period
n: The reviewer names harmony, proportion, and human-centered design as what Vitruvius emphasised.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: What name is given to the transitional space — between "here" and "there" — that sits between public and private realms?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Threshold
n: Threshold names the transitional space between here and there, or between the public and private realms. The reviewer treats it as a conceptual term rather than a physical door sill.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
q: Composed of angular concrete masses stepping down a hillside, the University of East Anglia (1962–68) is the work of which architect?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
n: Denys Lasdun designed the University of East Anglia. Paul Rudolph is the American counterpart named here, for the aggressively textured concrete facade of the Yale Art & Architecture Building (1963).

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: For which feature is the AT&T Building in New York (1978–84) especially known?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: Philip Johnson's AT&T Building sports a "Chippendale" broken pediment top — a giant ornamental surprise on a skyscraper, intended to make the building a distinctive corporate symbol.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Under which broader visual illusion does this reviewer group fictive architecture and quadratura as two techniques?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Trompe l'oeil
n: Trompe l'oeil is a visual illusion achieved artistically, particularly in painting, and the reviewer names fictive architecture and quadratura as the two such techniques used in architecture.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Roughly what date range does this reviewer give for Victorian architecture in Great Britain and the United States?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Victorian Architecture
n: The reviewer gives c. 1830 to c. 1901 for Victorian architecture, named after Queen Victoria. Revival and eclectic philosophies, particularly the Gothic revival, were a major force in the period.

s: Historical Development — Enlightenment and Neoclassicism
q: Which theorist (1713–1769) wrote Essai sur l'architecture (Essay on Architecture)?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Enlightenment & Neoclassicism: Marc-Antoine Laugier
n: Marc-Antoine Laugier, 1713–1769, wrote Essai sur l'architecture. Boullee and Ledoux are his contemporaries in this section but are treated as visionary designers rather than as the author of the Essai.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: The 1884 Home Insurance Building is cited as the earliest example of what building type?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: The Home Insurance Building (1884) is named as the first steel-frame skyscraper, one of the new building types made possible by advances in engineering and materials, alongside large expanses of glass.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: Beyond mere function, architectural theory in ancient times began to define what additional quality a structure should have?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period
n: The Ancient and Classical section states that theory began to define what makes a structure not only functional but beautiful and culturally significant.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: With which architect is the philosophy that a building should grow organically from its site most associated?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Organic Architecture
n: Organic architecture is associated with Frank Lloyd Wright. It emphasises the "integrity" of materials and a seamless transition between the interior and the exterior landscape.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Rejecting Modernism's strict functionalism in favor of emotional response through symbolic imagery and jagged lines, which primarily German early 20th-century style is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Expressionism
n: Expressionism emerged in the early 20th century primarily in Germany, using non-linear shapes, jagged lines, and often brick or early concrete to evoke emotional responses.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: During which two centuries, as defined here, was Colonial architecture — the architecture introduced to the western hemisphere from Europe — practiced?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Colonial Architecture
n: Colonial architecture covers what was introduced from Europe into the western hemisphere during the 17th and 18th centuries.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: In what year did Vignola's Regola delle cinque ordini d'architettura distill the proportions of the classical column?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola
n: Vignola distilled the column proportions in 1562, producing a handy canon of the Five Orders used as a textbook for centuries.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: In Venturi's distinction, what term describes a functional box carrying applied signage?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Duck vs. Decorated Shed
n: A Decorated Shed is the functional box with applied signage. A Duck is the opposite case — a building whose form is itself its ornament.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which 19th-century philosophy held that formal instruction at schools like the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris outranked a designer's own independent ideas?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Academicism
n: Academicism is about the authority of the school over the individual — the formal teaching of the Beaux-Arts is treated as the standard. Historicism is the near miss, but it names the use of past styles rather than deference to academic instruction.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: Which pair of architects designed the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris (1977)?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano designed the Pompidou, which turned architecture inside-out by placing structure and color-coded mechanical systems on the exterior.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which term describes design that meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Sustainability
n: That formula — present needs met without compromising future generations — is the reviewer's definition of sustainability. Biophilic design is about connection to nature for well-being, not intergenerational resource equity.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: A building earns praise for how well it fulfills its intended use — which element of the Vitruvian Triad does this concern?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period: Vitruvian Triad
n: Utilitas is functionality — how well the building serves its use. Firmitas concerns whether it stands up, and Venustas whether it pleases.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: In the Italian Renaissance, what did the word "casino" historically denote?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Casino
n: Historically a casino was a pavilion, lodge, or summerhouse common in the Italian Renaissance, or a place for dancing especially in the 18th century. The gambling hall meaning belongs only to the 20th century.

s: Definition of Terms — Planning and Landscape
q: Inspired by the planning seen at world's fairs, which early-1900s American movement favored greater use of parks, boulevards, and attractive waterfronts in town planning?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — City Beautiful Movement
n: The City Beautiful movement was the American early-1900s movement inspired by fair planning. The Garden City movement is the near miss, but it is English in origin and concerns planned suburban communities rather than civic beautification.

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: According to medieval theory, what does physical (Anagogical) light do?
o: Measures the passage of liturgical time
Determines the orientation of the nave
Reveals the true geometry of a structure
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period
n: Anagogical Light is the idea that physical light leads to divine light. Medieval theory paired it with the geometry of the "True Circle."

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: Beyond Vitruvius, Alberti argued that beauty was a matter of what — and that architecture was more than mere craft?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Leon Battista Alberti
n: Alberti argued beauty was a matter of Concinnitas, and treated architecture as a scientific and philosophical discipline rather than just a craft. Venustas is Vitruvius's own term and is exactly what Alberti moved beyond.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: For the Modern Movement, which three-part definition characterizes "modern" architecture?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Modern Movement
n: The Modern Movement, beginning in Europe c. 1900, defines modern architecture as that which is functional, rational, and nonhistorical.

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: Why, according to this reviewer, was medieval architectural theory not set down in formal treatises?
o: The classical texts had been lost
Theory was embedded in the religious and symbolic meanings of structures
Literacy was confined to the nobility
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period
n: Medieval architecture was largely symbolic and driven by theology, so theory was embedded in the religious and symbolic meanings of structures like cathedrals rather than set out in treatises.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Whose influence, in the early 20th century, was particularly strong for the grand-scale Beaux-Arts style in a specific region?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Beaux-Arts Style
n: The Beaux-Arts style, based on the historical and eclectic ideas taught in 19th-century Paris, had a particularly great influence in North America in the early 20th century.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Marked by extensive ribbing and ogee curves in tracery and arches, which style of English Gothic architecture is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 3–4: Definition of Terms — Decorated Style
n: Decorated Style covers English Gothic of the late 13th century and first half of the 14th, known for richness of decoration, extensive ribbing, and ogee curves in tracery and arches.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Described here as a primarily American style, Art Deco is marked by what formal quality?
o: Straight and angular lines with a sleekness of design
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Art Deco Style
n: Art Deco is marked by straight and angular lines and a sleekness of design, and was popular in the 1920s and 1930s. Organic and undulating lines belong to Art Nouveau, its immediate predecessor.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: In which century was Chinoiserie — the western European imitation of Chinese structures and design — most fashionable?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Chinoiserie
n: Chinoiserie, the western European imitative use of Chinese structures and design, was most fashionable in the 18th century.

s: Definition of Terms — Planning and Landscape
q: Under supervisors appointed by Parliament, more than two hundred Greek and Gothic Revival churches were erected in England during the two decades after 1818 — what is this period called?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Commissioners Era
n: The Commissioners Era covers the two decades after 1818, when over two hundred Greek and Gothic Revival churches were built under Commissioners appointed by Parliament.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: What term describes a carved frieze decorated with human and animal figures?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Historiated
n: Historiated means having human or animal figures as decorations. Biomorphic is the trap: it also draws on living things, but it abstracts their shapes and curves into a building's silhouette rather than depicting figures.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Palladianism's popularity in 18th-century England owed partly to the publications of whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Palladianism
n: Palladianism is a revival based on the buildings and publications of Andrea Palladio, and its 18th-century English popularity is credited partially to the publications of Lord Burlington. It is sometimes called Palladian classicism.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Under which philosophy does this glossary cite Frampton's "Towards a Critical Regionalism"?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Regionalism (Frampton, "Towards a Critical Regionalism")
n: Regionalism emphasises the architectural characteristics of a particular region through local forms and materials, or by designing so as to develop the potential of the regional style — the reviewer cites Frampton for it.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: In eastern North America, Colonial architecture is identified by which set of styles?
o: Dutch Colonial, Georgian, or New England style
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Colonial Architecture
n: Eastern North America gives Dutch Colonial, Georgian, or the New England style. Spanish and Portuguese styles are the meaning in Latin America and the southwestern United States — the geographic split is the point of the entry.

s: Definition of Terms — Planning and Landscape
q: Standing in direct contrast to the highly planned French formal garden, what is the 18th- and 19th-century "gardenesque" landscaping style also known as?
o: The highly planned French formal garden
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Garden Style
n: Garden style emphasises an informal, picturesque quality and is in direct contrast to the highly planned French formal garden.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: Which four elements did 1970s postmodern architecture bring back into building design?
o: Proportion, symmetry, the orders, and the module
Color, ornament, historical reference, and irony
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: Color, ornament, historical reference, and irony — the four things modernism had set aside, brought back as a rejection of its austerity.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: During which decades did the International Style rise to become a global architectural language?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: The reviewer places the style's rise to a global language of architecture in the 1940s and 50s.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: By the 1910s and 1920s, modernist ideals had come together in Europe and the U.S. through which two movements?
o: The Vienna Secession and the Catalan School
CIAM in Switzerland and MIAR in Italy
Constructivism in Russia and Purism in France
De Stijl in the Netherlands and the Bauhaus in Germany
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: De Stijl in the Netherlands and the Bauhaus in Germany are the two the reviewer names for this consolidation.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Especially in which country was Romanticism, as a stylistic philosophy, popular in the late 19th century?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Romanticism
n: The reviewer places late 19th-century Romanticism especially in Germany. Its major movement, Romantic classicism, was already established by the late 18th century and ran to about 1850.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Which pair of individuals makes up Coop Himmelblau, named among the key Deconstructivist practices?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: Coop Himmelblau is Wolf Prix and Helmut Swiczinsky. The other pairs are real partnerships but belong to Brutalism, contemporary digital design, and High-Tech respectively.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: Through what means did International Style architecture achieve its visually weightless quality?
o: Load-bearing masonry set back at each floor
Exposed structural frames on the exterior
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Cantilevers and light materials produced the visually weightless quality, alongside rectilinear forms, taut planar surfaces without ornament, and open interior spaces.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: According to this reviewer, expressions of historicism grew rare following which two developments?
o: The decline of Beaux-Arts and the beginning of the Modern movement
The rise of Art Nouveau and the Vienna Secession
The Chicago School and the invention of the skyscraper
The end of the Victorian era and the First World War
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Historicism
n: Historicism is the philosophy of using past historical styles and features. The reviewer states there has been little expression of it since the Beaux-Arts style declined and the Modern movement began.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: Which idea from Vitruvius does Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man illustrate?
o: The golden ratio applied to facades
Anthropomorphic proportions harmonising the human body and architectural design
The primitive hut as the origin of building
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period
n: The Vitruvian Man exemplifies Vitruvius's anthropomorphic proportions, emphasising the harmony between the human body and architectural design. The primitive hut belongs to Laugier, centuries later.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: Which tools are now considered routine for producing forms of previously unattainable complexity?
o: Advanced 3D modeling, parametric algorithms, and AI-driven tools
Structural analysis software and BIM clash detection
Hand drafting, physical models, and photogrammetry
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends: Digital and Parametric Design
n: Advanced 3D modeling, parametric algorithms, and even AI-driven tools, building on the late-20th-century computational experiments.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: With which collaborator did Mies design the 1958 Seagram Building, a bronze-and-glass tower set back on its plaza?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Mies designed the Seagram Building with Philip Johnson. The reviewer calls it "the most chaste" and most refined of the postwar modernist office buildings.

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: Over what span of centuries does this reviewer place the Medieval period?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period
n: The reviewer dates the Medieval period from the 5th to the 15th century CE.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: Which firm designed Lever House (1952) in New York?
o: Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed Lever House (1952). With Eero Saarinen's General Motors Technical Center (1948–56), it was an early exemplar of the sleek, geometric modern corporate campus.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: In the Vitruvian Triad, which term denotes structural soundness?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period: Vitruvian Triad
n: Firmitas is structural integrity, Utilitas is functionality, and Venustas is aesthetics or beauty. Concinnitas is not part of the triad at all — it is Alberti's later addition to the theory of beauty.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: In the Philippines, what were skilled but unlicensed builders of the Spanish colonial era — who both designed and supervised projects — called?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Maestro de Obras
n: Maestro de obras means "master builder." The reviewer treats them as the forerunner to modern architects: they managed laborers, ensured quality, and bridged the gap between design and construction despite being unlicensed.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: The International Style gained wide recognition in connection with which 1932 event?
o: The International Exhibition of Modern Architecture in New York
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms: International Style
n: The 1932 International Exhibition of Modern Architecture in New York gave the style its wide recognition. First identified by the term in the 1930s, it was described as functional, nontraditional, and nonregional, and practised worldwide in the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Reviving regional art and absorbing Art Nouveau under a local name, which late-1880s-to-early-1900s Catalan movement is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Catalan School
n: The Catalan School absorbed the new Art Nouveau style locally called Modernismo. Renaixensa Catalan is the regional art revival it also focused on — a related but distinct part of the same entry.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Originating in late 19th-century France, which educational system placed students in the studios of practicing architects who also served as faculty?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Atelier Concept
n: The atelier concept placed students in the studios of faculty members who were successful practising architects. Academicism is the related philosophy, but the atelier is the specific educational system.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
q: For which quality is Paul Rudolph's 1963 Yale Art & Architecture Building especially noted?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
n: The Yale Art & Architecture Building presents an aggressively textured concrete facade — the American statement of Brutalism in this section.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: By which title is Vitruvius's codification of architecture into a treatise known?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period
n: De Architectura, the Ten Books on Architecture, is the work of Vitruvius, a Roman architect and engineer. De Re Aedificatoria is Alberti's, and I Quattro Libri is Palladio's.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which pair of glossary terms respectively names a project's overall concept and its rough initial sketch?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 4–5: Definition of Terms — Esquisse; Parti
n: Parti is the overall concept for an architectural project; esquisse is the rough sketch done at the beginning, comparable to a written outline for a literary work. The order matters — reversing them is the common slip.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: What term describes creating an illusion through decorative or artistic techniques such as perspective?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 4–5: Definition of Terms — Illusionism
n: Illusionism is the general term for creating an illusion by decorative or artistic technique. Quadratura and trompe l'oeil are specific techniques of illusionism, not the umbrella term.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Who is credited with making the late 19th-century English Arts and Crafts movement famous?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Arts and Crafts Movement
n: William Morris made the Arts and Crafts movement famous. It emphasised quality of design and handcrafted products, and is sometimes referred to as the "craftsman" style.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Which local heritage partly inspired the angular, anthropomorphic exterior of the Guggenheim Bilbao?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: The shipbuilding heritage of the region inspired the exterior — the metal surfaces resemble ship hulls — and the building provided a "dynamic new image" for the industrial city of Bilbao.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: Which three qualities did Walter Gropius emphasize in merging art, design, and industrial technology?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Walter Gropius
n: Gropius, founder of the Bauhaus School, emphasised standardization, rationality, and functionality.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
q: Which 1952 raw-concrete housing block by Le Corbusier in Marseille went on to influence designers worldwide?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
n: The Unite d'Habitation in Marseille (1952) is the raw concrete housing block that influenced designers worldwide. Villa Savoye is his International Style villa of two decades earlier.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: Which campus and which private house are credited to Mies in this section?
o: The Bauhaus Dessau campus and the Fagus House
The University of East Anglia and the Steiner House
The Illinois Institute of Technology campus and the Farnsworth House
The General Motors Technical Center and the Tugendhat House
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Mies created the Illinois Institute of Technology campus and the Farnsworth House. The General Motors Technical Center is Eero Saarinen's.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: What term describes architecture representative of local or regional building types using traditional materials?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Vernacular Architecture
n: Vernacular architecture is representative of local or regional types and uses traditional materials. Regionalism is the near miss — it is a philosophy that deliberately develops the potential of a regional style, rather than the traditional building itself.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
q: Who coined the term "New Brutalism" for their uncompromising 1950s British designs?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
n: Alison and Peter Smithson coined "New Brutalism." Their Hunstanton School (1949–54) used austere brick and concrete with exposed structural elements, borrowing the strict clarity of Mies van der Rohe's approach.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: Reflecting shifts in which four areas does this reviewer frame the historical development of architectural theory, from ancient ideals to modern critiques?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8; Historical Development of the Theory of Architecture
n: The four named drivers are philosophy, culture, technology, and society. This framing is what the whole historical section is organised around.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: First used in the late 1870s, in which decade did Shingle style become popular on both American coasts and in the Midwest?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Shingle Style
n: The reviewer dates the first use to the late 1870s and its popularity on both coasts and in the Midwest to the 1880s.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: Which Chicago architect, advocating utilitarian simplicity, declared "form follows function"?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: Louis Sullivan, a Chicago architect and the most prominent figure of the Chicago School, declared "form follows function."

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: Respectively based on a square and an equilateral triangle, what are the Master Mason's Ad Quadratum and Ad Triangulum design methods built upon?
o: A square and an equilateral triangle
A square and a golden rectangle
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period: The Master Mason
n: Ad Quadratum designs on a square; Ad Triangulum designs on an equilateral triangle. For the Master Mason, theory was practical and geometric rather than philosophical.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Which set of three priorities correctly defines the International Style?
o: Mass over volume, regularity over symmetry, rejection of ornament
Volume over mass, regularity over symmetry, rejection of ornament
Volume over mass, symmetry over regularity, restrained ornament
Mass over volume, symmetry over regularity, applied ornament
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms: International Style
n: Volume over mass, regularity over symmetry, and the rejection of ornament. Reversing the first two pairs is the classic error — the style privileges the enclosed volume and the regular rhythm, not the solid mass or the axial symmetry.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Definition and Origins
q: What earlier trend did modern architecture arise as a pushback against?
o: The engineering excesses of the industrial age
The eclectic revival of past styles in the 19th century
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Architecture in Modern Era
n: It was a reaction against the eclectic revival of past styles in the 19th century, driven by the belief that the modern age required a radically new architectural expression for "modern man."

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Showing the influence of which building type, does Sukiya architecture use unfinished materials to create a natural effect?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Sukiya
n: Sukiya shows the influence of the traditional teahouse, including the use of unfinished materials to create a natural effect.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: What does Learning from Las Vegas (1972) claim to be a rediscovery of?
o: The commercial logic of the American strip
The engineering honesty of industrial structures
The vernacular building traditions of the American Southwest
The various meanings contained within the mainly classical architecture of the past
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Robert Venturi
n: The reviewer frames the book as the rediscovery of the various meanings contained within the mainly classical architecture of the past, and their application to modern structures.

s: Historical Development — Enlightenment and Neoclassicism
q: What character of architecture did visionary theorists Etienne-Louis Boullee and Claude-Nicolas Ledoux describe?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Enlightenment & Neoclassicism
n: Boullee and Ledoux theorized monumental, abstract, and symbolic architecture.

s: Historical Development — Ancient and Classical Period
q: For which periods do Vitruvian principles lay a foundational cornerstone, according to this reviewer?
o: The Renaissance and even modern architecture
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Ancient and Classical Period
n: The reviewer says Vitruvius's principles laid the foundation for Renaissance and even modern architecture — the reason his triad still appears in contemporary theory.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: Which benefit justifies the long horizontal or ribbon windows called for in the Five Points?
o: Reduced solar gain on the south face
The best illumination and ventilation, lighting the room end to end
Visual continuity with the roof garden
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Five Points of Architecture
n: Ribbon windows provide the best illumination and ventilation and would light the room from end to end.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Emphasizing an organic relationship between individual buildings and parts of an urban area, which style is associated with a group formed in Tokyo in 1960?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Metabolism
n: Metabolism is associated with a group formed in Tokyo in 1960, emphasising the organic relationship between individual buildings and between different parts of an urban area.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: The Renaissance is said to mark the separation of which two professional roles?
o: The master mason and the guild
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period
n: The era marks the separation of the "Architect," the designer, from the "Builder," the executor. This is what the Renaissance revival of Vitruvian principles infused with Humanism produced in practice.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: Which discovery enabled Renaissance architects to conceptualize space theoretically before it was ever built?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period
n: The discovery of linear perspective let architects theorize space before construction. Theory then became obsessed with the "Ideal City" and centralized, symmetrical plans such as the Greek Cross.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Which architect does this reviewer name under BOTH Deconstructivism and Contemporary Theory, also crediting them with parametric and fluid design?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 12, 14: Contemporary Theory; Deconstructivism
n: Zaha Hadid appears among the Deconstructivists, as the first woman to win the Pritzker, and again under Parametricism for her later fluid geometries. Gehry, Eisenman, and Libeskind appear only in the Deconstructivism discussion.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: How does this glossary define "colorism," in its simplest terms?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Colorism
n: The reviewer gives colorism a one-line definition: the use of color. Nothing about symbolism or theory is attached to the term here.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: The Chicago School's best-known architect is identified as whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Chicago School
n: Louis Sullivan was the Chicago School's most prominent architect. The movement of the mid-1880s and 1890s is characterised by nonhistoricism, steel framing, and the dominance of vertical and horizontal lines.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Characterized by a low roof, rounded windows, and an informal winged plan based on rural Italian (especially Tuscan) models, which 19th-century country-house style is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 7–8: Definition of Terms — Villa Style
n: Villa style was used for prominent country houses in Britain and the United States, based on rural Italian models particularly in Tuscany, with a low roof, rounded windows, and an informal plan with wings.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: Who designed the 1910 Steiner House, an austere, unadorned concrete form and one of the earliest private houses built of reinforced concrete?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: Adolf Loos in Vienna opposed all applied ornament, and his 1910 Steiner House was one of the first private houses of reinforced concrete.

s: Historical Development — Contemporary Theory (21st Century)
q: Which architect wrote S, M, L, XL, and what subject does it address?
o: Charles Jencks — the language of postmodernism
Rem Koolhaas — the modern city's scale and complexity
Patrik Schumacher — parametricism as a style
Zaha Hadid — parametric and fluid design
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Contemporary Theory: Rem Koolhaas
n: Rem Koolhaas's S, M, L, XL speaks to the modern city's scale and complexity that defy traditional humanist design, exploring urbanism, globalization, and the chaos of contemporary space.

s: Historical Development — Enlightenment and Neoclassicism
q: What does "architecture parlante," as proposed by Boullee and Ledoux, translate to?
o: Speaking architecture, where form reflects function
Silent architecture, where ornament is banished
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Enlightenment & Neoclassicism
n: Architecture parlante means speaking architecture, where form reflects function. It is an Enlightenment ancestor of the later modernist slogan, arrived at through symbolism rather than efficiency.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: Under which of Venturi's categories does a building whose own form serves as its ornament fall?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Duck vs. Decorated Shed
n: A Duck is a building whose form is its ornament. Novelty architecture is the tempting distractor from the glossary, but it specifically means buildings shaped like inanimate man-made objects for advertising — narrower than the Duck.

s: Historical Development — 19th Century: Romanticism, Historicism and the Industrial Age
q: Beyond truth to materials and craftsmanship, what third quality did Ruskin emphasize in architecture?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: 19th Century: John Ruskin
n: Ruskin emphasised truth to materials, craftsmanship, and moral responsibility. He advocated for Gothic Revival and condemned industrialization's impact on design quality.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which Latin term, rendered in English as "spirit of the place," names a location's unique atmosphere?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Genius Loci
n: Genius loci translates as "genius of the place" or "spirit of the place" and refers to the unique spirit or atmosphere a place possesses.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: In what year did an exposition held in Paris give rise to the term Art Deco?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Art Deco Style
n: The term comes from the 1925 Paris Exposition Internationale des Arts Decoratifs et Industriels. The 1932 date belongs to the New York exhibition that popularised the International Style — a common mix-up.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
q: By what means does London City Hall (2002) achieve self-shading?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
n: London City Hall's tilted form provides self-shading — one of Foster's sustainable projects alongside the Commerzbank Tower.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: In place of ornamentation and historical styles, which three things did Modernism favor?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism (Early–Mid 20th Century)
n: Function, efficiency, and new materials. Symbolism, irony, and plurality are exactly what Postmodernism later reintroduced against this.

s: Definition of Terms — Planning and Landscape
q: Which combination of elements did the early 20th-century Garden City movement plan for its suburban communities?
o: Civic buildings, residences, parks, and agricultural areas
Industrial estates, workers' housing, and rail links
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Garden City Movement
n: The Garden City movement planned suburban communities containing civic buildings, residences, parks, and agricultural areas. It was strongest in England and later Germany.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: In which country did Baroque architecture originate at the start of the 17th century?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Baroque Architecture
n: The Baroque started in Italy at the beginning of the 17th century and was later practised in areas of Germany and Austria into the 18th century. Germany and Austria are where it spread, not where it began.

s: Historical Development — Enlightenment and Neoclassicism
q: By the 17th century, European architectural theory had begun absorbing which three Enlightenment ideals?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Enlightenment & Neoclassicism
n: Reason, science, and progress. Alongside these came a burgeoning interest in history and archaeology, pushing architecture towards rationality, idealism, and universal truths.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: According to this reviewer, Mies van der Rohe's dictum holds that form follows what?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Modernism: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
n: For Mies, form follows structure — a deliberate variant on Sullivan's form follows function, and the reason his glass-and-steel buildings read as expressions of their frames.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Greek Revival, Federal Revival, and Roman Revival are identified as specific expressions of which broader early 19th-century movement?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Classical Revival
n: Classical Revival was an early 19th-century movement, particularly in England and the United States, based on ancient Greek and Roman models; Greek, Federal, and Roman Revival are its named specific forms.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: As a glossary entry, "high tech style" is defined as design whose shapes, materials, and surfaces reflect what?
o: The honesty of exposed structure alone
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — High Tech Style
n: The glossary entry defines high tech style by shapes, materials, and surfaces reflecting the latest developments in technology — a broader definition than the later section's account of exposed services and steel frameworks.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: By what alternative name is Gothic Revival also known?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Gothic Revival
n: The reviewer states that Gothic Revival is also called neo-Gothic. It ran through the late 18th and 19th centuries in Europe and North America and continued into the 20th century in church and collegiate architecture.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Beyond the 15th century, what additional span does Renaissance architecture in Italy cover?
o: The first half of the 17th century
The second half of the 14th century
The first half of the 16th century
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms: Renaissance Architecture
n: In Italy the Renaissance covers the 15th century and the first half of the 16th. Elsewhere in Europe it runs later — from the mid-16th century through the early 17th.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Whose early work is the Vitra Fire Station in Germany (1989–93), which slices space with sharp oblique planes to suggest frozen movement?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: The Vitra Fire Station is Zaha Hadid's early work, creating a sense of frozen movement through sharp, oblique planes.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: Which architect (1404–1472) is known as the "Vitruvius of the Renaissance"?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Leon Battista Alberti
n: Leon Battista Alberti, 1404–1472, is the "Vitruvius of the Renaissance." Palladio, born 1508, carries a different title — father of modern picture books of architecture.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Alongside whom did Le Corbusier develop Purism in 1918, as a reaction against Cubism?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Purism
n: Purism was developed in 1918 by Amedee Ozenfant and Le Corbusier in reaction to Cubism, favouring simplicity and machine aesthetic.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
q: Which of the following is NOT listed among this reviewer's key strategies for sustainable architecture?
o: Exposing structural services as aesthetic features
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
n: Exposing services as aesthetic features is a High-Tech trademark, not a sustainability strategy. The listed strategies are insulation and daylight optimization, renewable energy systems, rainwater collection, green roofs and living walls, natural ventilation, and recycled or local materials.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: Gropius, Le Corbusier, and Mies van der Rohe share which common experience?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: All three worked in Peter Behrens's office, which is why the reviewer credits him with mentoring a generation of modernists.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: How did High-Tech architects extend the modernist fascination with materials and structure?
o: Concealing structure behind taut planar surfaces
Applying historical ornament to industrial forms
Literally exposing and celebrating a building's technological components
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: They literally exposed and celebrated the building's technological components — the opposite of the International Style's taut, unbroken planar surfaces.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: MoMA's landmark 1988 show "Deconstructivist Architecture" framed the angular spatial forms on display as visible expressions of which concept?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: The exhibit described them as "tangible realizations of chaos theory," reminiscent in some ways of the irregular forms of Russian Constructivism and German Expressionism from the 1920s.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: Combining modern technology with traditional or historical motifs, Double Coding serves what purpose?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Double Coding (Jencks)
n: Double Coding communicates with different audiences at once — the professional reading the modern technology and the public reading the historical motif. It is the mechanism behind Jencks's "pluralistic and double-coded" definition.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: Dramatically cantilevered over a waterfall in 1935, which house exemplifies an architect's philosophy of merging architecture with nature?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: Fallingwater (1935) exemplifies Frank Lloyd Wright's "organic" approach to modernism, integrating architecture with nature.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which single term describes a sculpture-like quality in a design?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Plasticity
n: Plasticity is defined in this glossary as a sculpture-like quality. Tectonic is the neighbouring term but concerns construction and buildings rather than sculptural character.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Emphasizing geometric shapes and industrial materials, which Russian movement of the 1920s proved especially influential in design?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Constructivism
n: Constructivism is the Russian movement of the 1920s emphasising geometric shapes and industrial materials. Socialist realism is the trap — it is also Russian, but it is the official U.S.S.R. style from the 1930s onward.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Named as ornamentation marking the beginning of the Renaissance in England, strapwork and mulling decoration belong to which style?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Elizabethan Architecture
n: Elizabethan architecture, in the second half of the 16th century and named for Queen Elizabeth I, represents the beginning of Renaissance architecture in England and exhibits strapwork and mulling decoration.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Which two English architects are credited as influences on the American Shingle style?
o: Charles Voysey and R. Norman Shaw
R. Norman Shaw and Philip Webb
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Shingle Style
n: Influences on the Shingle style were American colonial buildings and the work of English architects R. Norman Shaw and Philip Webb. The style is marked by shingles on both roofs and walls, and an informality and fluidity in exterior wall surfaces.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: Which architect wrote both Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966) and Learning from Las Vegas (1972)?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Robert Venturi
n: Both are Robert Venturi's. Jencks is the other postmodern theorist here, but his major work is The Language of Postmodern Architecture.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: For what purpose is pilotis — the French term for piles rising above ground level — used?
o: Open space at the ground level
A free facade in the vertical plane
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Pilotis
n: Pilotis support the structure while creating open space at the ground level. The roof garden and the free facade are separate items in Le Corbusier's Five Points, each with its own purpose.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: What are the two phases of the Decorated style called?
o: The Early English and the Perpendicular
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Decorated Style
n: The Decorated style has two phases, the Geometric and the Curvilinear. Early English and Perpendicular are the styles that bracket it — Decorated followed the former and preceded the latter.

s: Historical Development — Enlightenment and Neoclassicism
q: As what did Laugier propose the "Primitive Hut"?
o: The earliest form of the classical temple
An allegory of the social contract
A model for rural housing reform
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Enlightenment & Neoclassicism: Marc-Antoine Laugier
n: Laugier proposed the Primitive Hut as the origin of all architecture, arguing that architecture should return to its essential elements: the column, the entablature, and the pediment.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
q: Which sustainable device is used by the Commerzbank Tower in Frankfurt (1997)?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
n: Norman Foster's Commerzbank Tower uses sky-gardens for cooling. The tilted form for self-shading belongs to his London City Hall of 2002 — the two are easily swapped.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: According to the "Machine for Living" concept, what should a house be?
o: An organism grown from its site
A tool designed for maximum efficiency
A shelter stripped of all ornament
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Le Corbusier
n: The Machine for Living treats the house as a tool designed for maximum efficiency. The organism growing from its site is Wright's organic architecture — the opposing view of the same period.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Which late 20th-century movement does this reviewer describe as having the appearance of "controlled chaos"?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms: Deconstructivism
n: Deconstructivism challenges traditional ideas of stability and geometry and is characterised by fragmentation, non-rectilinear shapes, and an appearance of "controlled chaos."

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: Which building is cited as the exemplar of cities pursuing iconic architecture to put themselves "on the map"?
