ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends: Globalization and "Starchitects"
n: The Guggenheim Bilbao is the exemplar, followed by subsequent cultural projects such as Dubai's museum boom and China's avant-garde opera houses.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Featuring skewed grids and fragmented forms, the 1989 Wexner Center for the Arts at Ohio State University was designed by whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: Peter Eisenman designed the Wexner Center, whose skewed grids make the building read as a deconstructed collage of spaces.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: In which two countries was Art Nouveau popularized during the 1890s?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Art Nouveau
n: Art Nouveau was popularised in France and Belgium in the 1890s. Germany, Austria, Italy, and Spain each had counterpart movements under different names.

s: Historical Development — Contemporary Theory (21st Century)
q: Beyond advancing parametric and fluid design, which distinction does Zaha Hadid hold?
o: First non-European to win the Pritzker Prize
First woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize
First architect to use CAD in practice
First deconstructivist to design a museum
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Contemporary Theory: Zaha Hadid
n: Zaha Hadid was the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize, and she advanced parametric and fluid design that challenged spatial norms.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: Featuring a diagrid exoskeleton, the 1985 HSBC Headquarters in Hong Kong is the work of which High-Tech leader?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: Norman Foster designed the HSBC Headquarters with its diagrid exoskeleton, and also the Sainsbury Centre (1978) — both pioneering lightweight structures.

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: Cairo's 9th-century Ibn Tulun Mosque is offered as an example of structural innovations that fed into which later tradition?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period: Structural Logic
n: Under structural logic, the pointed arch and other innovations used in mosques such as the Ibn Tulun Mosque later influenced European Gothic design, as engineering and geometric knowledge flourished in the Islamic world.

s: Historical Development — 19th Century: Romanticism, Historicism and the Industrial Age
q: Which three forces are named as driving the divergence in 19th-century architectural thought?
o: Industrial technology, Romanticism, and historic revivals
Academicism, the atelier, and the Beaux-Arts
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 9–10: 19th Century
n: The rise of industrial technology, Romanticism, and historic revivals led to the divergence. Adherents held that Gothic architecture represented a more "honest" and Christian society than the "pagan" Classical style.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: What term describes placing dissimilar elements side by side to highlight their contrasting qualities?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Juxtaposition
n: Juxtaposition is the strategic side-by-side placement of dissimilar elements, used to sharpen contrast or produce a unique visual effect.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: Originating and developed most fully in France during the 18th century, which style used extensive, usually light and elegant decoration with natural motifs?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Rococo Architecture
n: Rococo originated and developed most fully in France in the 18th century, with light, elegant, richly decorated interiors employing natural motifs. The Baroque is the near miss but is Italian in origin and heavier in character.

s: Historical Development — 19th Century: Romanticism, Historicism and the Industrial Age
q: Which critic (1819–1900) wrote The Seven Lamps of Architecture?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: 19th Century: John Ruskin
n: John Ruskin, 1819–1900, wrote The Seven Lamps of Architecture. Viollet-le-Duc is the other 19th-century figure in this section but is known for Gothic restorations and rational analysis rather than for the Seven Lamps.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: Responding to Modernism's coldness, which three things did Postmodernism embrace?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
n: Symbolism, irony, and plurality are the three the reviewer names as Postmodernism's answer to modernist coldness.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: Based on which two references is Le Modulor, an anthropometric scale of proportions, constructed?
o: The human body and the metric system
The human body and the golden ratio
The human stride and the module of the column
The classical orders and the golden ratio
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Le Modulor
n: Le Modulor, devised by Le Corbusier, is based on the human body and the golden ratio.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: First meeting in Switzerland in 1928, in what year did CIAM disband?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — C.I.A.M.
n: CIAM disbanded in 1956. It was committed to functionalist aesthetics and had representatives in west European countries. 1933 is the closing of the Bauhaus, not of CIAM.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which modernist architect popularized Biorealism, the study of the relationship between the human nervous system and the built environment?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Biorealism
n: Biorealism was popularised by modernist architect Richard Neutra, and the reviewer calls it arguably the precursor to modern environmental psychology.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: Featuring a steel frame and curtain walls, the 1911 Fagus Factory was designed by whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: Walter Gropius's Fagus Factory (1911) exemplified the new aesthetic of functional industrial design with no historical ornament. He went on to found the Bauhaus school in 1919.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
q: Which Malaysian architect championed bioclimatic skyscrapers that integrate vegetation and natural airflow?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
n: Ken Yeang from Malaysia championed bioclimatic skyscrapers that integrate vegetation and natural airflow.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which 20th-century philosophy emphasizes a building's uses while revealing its structure and materials, becoming a major principle of the International Style?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Functionalism
n: Functionalism ties the design to the building's uses and lets structure and materials show. The reviewer names it explicitly as a major principle of the International Style.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Built 1989–99 as a zig-zagging, lightning-bolt form with slashed window voids meant to convey the fractured history of Jewish life in Germany, which building is this?
o: The Wexner Center for the Arts
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: Daniel Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin uses the zig-zagging lightning-bolt form and slashed window voids to convey the fractured history of Jewish life in Germany.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: Which 1508–1580 architect earned the title "father of modern picture books of architecture"?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Andrea Palladio
n: Andrea Palladio, 1508–1580, is called the father of modern picture books of architecture, on the strength of I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: By what name were the artists who practiced illusionistic ceiling or wall painting during the baroque period known?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Quadratura
n: Quadratura is the ceiling or wall painting that creates an illusion, and the artists who practised it in the baroque period were called quadraturista.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: For what did Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture criticize modernism?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism: Robert Venturi
n: The book criticized modernism for being too simplistic and austere, and was a key influence on the development of Postmodernism.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: By what other name is the late 19th-century revival of North American Colonial architecture also known?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Colonial Revival
n: Colonial Revival is also called the neo-Colonial style and refers to the late 19th-century revival of North American Colonial architecture.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: In which material is the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (1991–1997) clad?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao is an explosion of curvilinear forms clad in titanium panels, described as having "curved walls and pillar-less open spaces [that] defy the laws of physics."

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Evolution of Modern Architecture
q: Which pioneer of modern industrial architecture designed the 1909 AEG Turbine Factory?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Evolution of Modern Architecture
n: Peter Behrens in Germany pioneered modern industrial architecture with the AEG Turbine Factory (1909). Gropius is the near miss — his Fagus Factory is 1911, and he was one of Behrens's protégés.

s: Definition of Terms — Planning and Landscape
q: From what source did the Picturesque movement in English landscape architecture draw its taste for informal, rugged, "sublime" scenes?
o: The informal, rugged, and "sublime" scenes depicted in French paintings
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 5–6: Definition of Terms — Picturesque Movement
n: Picturesque taste is based upon the informal, sometimes rugged, and "sublime" scenes depicted in French paintings — which is why the Sublime and the Picturesque appear together in this glossary.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: In its strict sense, what did the Queen Anne style revive?
o: Simple vernacular forms used in England in the early 18th century
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Queen Anne Style
n: Strictly the Queen Anne revives the simple vernacular architectural forms used in England in the early 18th century. The term is also loosely used in the United States for houses based on Elizabethan and Tudor models — that looser usage is the distractor.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Which monarch invited Italian architects, stuccoists, and mural painters to decorate a French royal palace in the 1530s?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — School of Fontainebleau
n: King Francis I invited them to decorate his palace at Fontainebleau in the 1530s. The group is sometimes called the "First School" to distinguish it from a later group, and its richness made it a major influence on Renaissance decoration elsewhere in Europe.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: In what year was the exhibition society that gave the term "Arts and Crafts" its name founded?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Arts and Crafts Movement
n: The term originated with the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, founded in 1888.

s: Definition of Terms — Planning and Landscape
q: In town planning, what term names a band of parks or open land kept protected from development?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Greenbelt
n: A greenbelt is a band of parks or open land protected from development.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: From which French phrase does the term Brutalism derive?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 2–3: Definition of Terms: Brutalism
n: Brutalism derives from beton brut, meaning raw concrete, and is known alternately as New Brutalism. The style dates to the 1950s and emphasises raw forms of concrete, often heavy and/or dark.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: Whose Tutte l'opere d'architettura broke down the classical orders through practical illustrations, making Vitruvian ideas accessible to craftsmen?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Sebastiano Serlio
n: Sebastiano Serlio's Tutte l'opere d'architettura did this, and also addressed stage design and perspective, bridging architecture and theater.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: What term names Rossi's study and classification of building types by shared formal or functional characteristics?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Typology (Rossi, The Architecture of the City)
n: Typology is the study and classification of building types by shared formal or functional characteristics, credited here to Rossi's The Architecture of the City.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: In the early 20th century, architectural theory became a tool for what purpose?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism (Early–Mid 20th Century)
n: The reviewer states that theory became a tool for social engineering, with the focus shifting to efficiency, hygiene, and the rejection of historical ornament.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: By placing which elements on the exterior did the 1986 Lloyd's Building free up its interior?
o: Service cores — stairwells, elevators, and pipes
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: Richard Rogers's Lloyd's Building placed service cores — stairwells, elevators, pipes — on the outside, freeing the interior and giving the building a slick, engineered appearance.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: With which architect is the phrase "less is more" associated?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Modernism: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
n: Mies van der Rohe championed minimalism and is known for "Less is more," focusing on minimalist glass-and-steel architecture where form follows structure. Loos is the near miss — he opposed ornament, but the phrase is not his.

s: Historical Development — Medieval Period
q: By what phrase were Gothic cathedrals — viewed as buildings that preach — described?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 8: Medieval Period: Architecture as Theology
n: Under architecture as theology, buildings — particularly Gothic cathedrals — were seen as "sermons in stone." Heavenly Jerusalem is the related but distinct idea of what the height and light were meant to represent.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: In what way were strict Functionalist principles increasingly felt to have failed?
o: They had failed to withstand the climate
They had failed to create a humane environment and caused visual damage to historic cities
They had failed to reduce construction costs
They had failed to accommodate the automobile
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: The reviewer quotes both charges: functionalism had "failed to create a humane environment" in new cities and had caused "visual damage to historic cities," as tower blocks and megastructures ignored context.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Which trend has been identified as the turning away from Modern Movement values during the 1960s and 1970s?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Modern Movement
n: The reviewer identifies the 1960s–1970s turning away from Modern Movement values as Postmodernism.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: Featuring an oversized gabled facade that playfully subverts traditional house forms, a small 1964 Philadelphia house was designed by whom, and for whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: The Vanna Venturi House (1964) is Robert Venturi's own house for his mother, and is the reviewer's key early example of postmodern subversion of traditional house forms.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: Which of Le Corbusier's Five Points restores the ground area that the house covers?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Five Points of Architecture
n: The roof garden restores, supposedly, the area of ground covered by the house. Pilotis is the point that elevates the mass off the ground — the two are complementary but distinct.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Popular in the 16th and 17th centuries, painting that renders architectural features so realistically they appear three-dimensional was especially favored in which country?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 4: Definition of Terms — Fictive Architecture
n: Fictive architecture — illusionistic painting of three-dimensional-looking architectural features — is placed by the reviewer in the 16th and 17th centuries, particularly in Italy.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: How is the open or free plan among Le Corbusier's Five Points achieved?
o: Separating the load-bearing columns from the walls that subdivide the space
Placing service cores on the exterior
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Five Points of Architecture
n: The free plan comes from separating the load-bearing columns from the walls that subdivide the space, so the partitions no longer carry load. The free facade is then the same outcome in the vertical plane.

s: Historical Development — 19th Century: Romanticism, Historicism and the Industrial Age
q: Introduced in the 18th and 19th centuries, what did Rationalism question, and what did this questioning eventually lead to?
o: How cities grow; the Garden City movement
Why buildings look the way they do; the radical break of the early 20th century
Whether ornament is moral; the Arts and Crafts movement
How buildings are financed; the rise of the corporate client
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: 19th Century
n: Rationalism questioned why buildings look the way they do, and the reviewer credits this line of questioning with leading to the radical break of the early 20th century.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: In Vers une architecture, Le Corbusier claimed the mass-produced house could be as beautiful as what?
o: The tools of the industry used to build it
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Le Corbusier
n: He stated the mass-produced house could be as beautiful as the tools of the industry that were used to build it. Vers une architecture is translated as Towards a New Architecture.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Taking its name from a journal, what does Jugendstil translate to?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Jugendstil
n: Jugendstil means "youth style" and comes from the Journal Jegend.

s: Historical Development — 19th Century: Romanticism, Historicism and the Industrial Age
q: Whose argument — that form should follow the logic of construction and materials — is credited with laying the groundwork for Modernism?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: 19th Century: Eugene Viollet-le-Duc
n: Viollet-le-Duc argued that form should follow the logic of construction and materials, laying the groundwork for Modernism. Sullivan's later "form follows function" is the descendant of this idea, not its source.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Definition and Origins
q: Which set of materials forms the basis of modern architecture's new mode of expression?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Architecture in Modern Era
n: Steel, glass, and reinforced concrete, coupled with a rejection of unnecessary ornament, characterise modern architecture as the reviewer defines it.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: Known as the "Bird's Nest," which practice designed the 2008 Beijing National Stadium?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
n: Herzog & de Meuron designed the Beijing National Stadium, whose lattice shell is cited alongside 3D-printed building prototypes as contemporary digital design.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
q: Which combination of qualities characterizes Brutalist architecture?
o: Taut planar surfaces, open interiors, and visual weightlessness
Exposed services, steel frameworks, and large expanses of glass
Fragmented forms, oblique planes, and dynamic tension
Massive monolithic forms, rough exposed concrete, and bold blocky geometries
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
n: Massive, monolithic forms; rough, exposed concrete surfaces; and bold, blocky geometries. The other three options describe the International Style, Deconstructivism, and High-Tech respectively.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: In which country was the bungalow — a one-storey frame dwelling often featuring a veranda — first used?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 3: Definition of Terms — Bungalow
n: The bungalow was first used in India and later became popular in England and the United States in the 20th century. The Arts and Crafts variant is the Craftsman bungalow.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: How was the Pompidou Centre described in relation to its historic setting?
o: "The most chaste" building of its era
A "dynamic new image" for the city
An "outrageous joke" in the historic city center
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: The reviewer records it as an "outrageous joke" in the historic city center — essentially a pop-art interpretation of high-tech ideas. "The most chaste" describes the Seagram Building, and "dynamic new image" the Guggenheim Bilbao.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: For which characteristic is the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku (2012) cited?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends: Digital and Parametric Design
n: The Heydar Aliyev Center is cited for its continuous swooping surfaces, exemplifying Parametricism. The lattice shell belongs to the Beijing National Stadium.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Producing architecture in a non-subjective, geometrical style using primary colors, which Dutch group of artists and designers, formed in 1917, is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 7: Definition of Terms — Stijl, De
n: De Stijl came together in 1917; its associated architecture is non-subjective and geometrical, emphasising space and using primary colors.

s: Historical Development — Modernism (Early to Mid 20th Century)
q: For which principle does this reviewer cite "The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered" as the source?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 10: Modernism: Functionalism (Sullivan)
n: Sullivan's essay is cited for Functionalism — the principle that the design of a building should be based solely on its purpose.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
q: Deconstructivism drew its philosophical inspiration from deconstruction, pioneered by which thinker?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Deconstructivism (1980s–1990s)
n: Jacques Derrida pioneered deconstruction; Deconstructivist architecture drew on it together with the avant-garde geometry of early 20th-century art.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Contemporary Trends (21st Century)
q: In what year was the Pritzker Prize, which highlighted the emerging global star system, established?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Contemporary Trends: Globalization and "Starchitects"
n: The Pritzker Prize was established in 1979, listing laureates from postmodernists to deconstructivists to high-tech pioneers. 1972 is the Pruitt-Igoe demolition and 1988 the MoMA Deconstructivist exhibit.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
q: Arranging classical columns and neon-lit arches within a fragmentary urban plaza, the Piazza d'Italia in New Orleans (1975–80) was designed by whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: Postmodernism (1970s–1990s)
n: Charles Moore designed the whimsical Piazza d'Italia, which directly engages historic imagery through classical columns and neon-lit arches.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Standing for the Italian branch of the 1920s–1930s Modern movement, what does the acronym MIAR stand for?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, pp. 6: Definition of Terms — Rationalist Movement
n: The Rationalist movement is known in Italy as the Movimento Italiano per l'Architectura Razionale, or MIAR.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: Through which two provisions does High-Tech design chiefly achieve flexibility and adaptability?
o: Deep plans and fixed service cores
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: Clear-span interiors and movable components are what give High-Tech buildings their flexibility and adaptability.

s: Definition of Terms — Design Philosophies and Concepts
q: Which theory concerns itself with how light, texture, and sound affect the soul rather than merely the eyes?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms — Phenomenology
n: Phenomenology focuses on human experience and the sensory perception of space. Biorealism is the near miss — it also links people and buildings, but through the nervous system as a study rather than through lived sensory experience.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: Beyond its methodology, to what else does this reviewer credit the Bauhaus's fame?
o: The development of a widely accepted functional aesthetic
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Bauhaus
n: The reviewer attributes the school's fame to its methodology and to the development of a widely accepted functional aesthetic — not to patronage or to ornament, which the Bauhaus set aside.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
q: By which two other names is High-Tech architecture also known?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 14: High-Tech Architecture (1970s–Present)
n: High-Tech is also known as Late Modern or Structural Expressionism.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
q: Reflecting Brutalism's social agenda, many of its projects belonged to which building types?
o: Public housing, government buildings, or universities
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: Brutalism (1950s–1970s)
n: Many Brutalist projects were public housing, government buildings, or universities, aiming for honest, unpretentious architecture for the masses.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: During which decade did the Modern movement gain acceptance in the United States, coinciding with a second phase of modernism?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 5: Definition of Terms — Modern Movement
n: A second phase of modernism occurred in the 1930s, which was also when the Modern movement gained acceptance in the United States with the onset of the international style.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Definition and Origins
q: Broadly defined, modern architecture emerged as an attempt to create a new nonhistorical architecture grounded in which two things?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 12: Architecture in Modern Era
n: It was grounded in Functionalism and modern building technology, emerging in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

s: Historical Development — Renaissance Period
q: Which of the following did Palladio introduce, expanding on Vitruvian ideas?
o: Modular design and classical orders, with emphasis on symmetry
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 9: Renaissance Period: Andrea Palladio
n: Palladio introduced modular design and classical orders and emphasised symmetry in villas and public buildings. The five points are Le Corbusier's, the primitive hut is Laugier's, and concinnitas is Alberti's.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — International Style (1920s–1950s)
q: The rise of curtain-walled skyscrapers and glass-box office towers worldwide is said to express a new aesthetic centered on what?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 13: International Style (1920s–1950s)
n: Corporate and institutional architecture embraced the style, reflecting a new aesthetic of rationalism and efficiency.

s: Definition of Terms — Modern Movements and Schools
q: After what was Art Nouveau sometimes called "style nouveau"?
o: A Paris shop that opened in 1895
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 2: Definition of Terms — Art Nouveau
n: The alternative name "style nouveau" came from the name of a Paris shop that opened in 1895. The style itself is marked by glass and metal, organic undulating lines, and a nonhistorical, often whimsical mood.

s: Definition of Terms — Historical Styles and Periods
q: The Italian word renascimento, from which the term Renaissance derives, refers to the rebirth of what?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 6: Definition of Terms: Renaissance Architecture
n: Renaissance refers to the rebirth (renascimento) of a classical taste, and the architecture shows a return to ancient Roman orders and architectural elements.

s: Architecture in the Modern Era — Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
q: Beyond efficient use of energy, water, and materials, what else does sustainable or "green" architecture aim to do?
o: Reducing the visual impact of buildings
Harmonizing with the climate and environment
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 15: Sustainable Architecture (1990s–Present)
n: Efficiency in energy, water, and materials plus harmonizing with the climate and environment are the two halves of the definition.

s: Historical Development — Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
q: According to this reviewer, how did postmodern buildings relate to function?
o: They were still meant to serve a function, as with modernism
They subordinated function to structural expression
They abandoned function in favour of symbolism
They treated function as purely decorative
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 1, p. 11: Postmodernism (Late 20th Century)
n: Postmodern buildings were still meant to serve a function, as with modernism. What changed was the rejection of the rigid rules dictating simplicity, abstraction, and simple shapes.
